title: Apple has a moldy core: why it can look fine on the outside

seo.title: Moldy core in an apple: why it happens and what to do
seo.meta_description: Mold can grow in an apple's seed cavity while the skin still looks normal. If you see fuzzy or powdery growth inside the core, the safest choice is to discard the apple.
seo.search_intent: Explain moldy core in apples, why it may be hidden from the outside, and what to do when it is discovered.

excerpt: An apple can develop mold in the seed cavity while its skin still looks firm and healthy. If cutting the fruit reveals fuzzy or powdery fungal growth in the core, discard the whole apple rather than simply scooping out the seeds and eating around it.
content_html:
The apple looks ordinary until you cut through the center and find white, gray, green, or dark fuzzy material around the seeds. Moldy core can develop inside the seed cavity before the peel gives you an obvious warning.

UC Davis identifies fungi including Alternaria, Fusarium, Aspergillus, and Penicillium as causes of moldy core in susceptible apples. Fruit with a more open calyx or sinus can be especially prone to this internal colonization.

How the outside can stay normal

The fungi may establish in the core cavity first. While the growth remains internal, flesh near the peel can still retain normal color and firmness, so squeezing or inspecting the skin cannot reliably rule it out.

Dark seeds by themselves are not mold. Mature apple seeds are naturally brown to almost black. Mold looks like growth on the cavity surface: fuzzy, cottony, or powdery material that is not part of the fruit's normal structure.

Do not just scoop out a moldy core

Once visible mold is growing inside moist fruit, you cannot tell by eye where microscopic growth or tissue damage ends. The practical household choice is to discard the apple rather than carve out the seed cavity and taste the surrounding flesh.

USDA food-mold guidance emphasizes that visible mold can be accompanied by growth beneath the surface, especially in moist foods. An internal cavity gives you even less confidence that the visible edge marks the true boundary.

Moldy core is different from plain browning

A firm brown patch can result from a physiological storage disorder. Fuzzy or powdery material around the seeds is a different finding. If mold is present, let that sign determine the decision even if the surrounding flesh still looks good.

What to look for

  • Dark seeds without fuzzy growth: can be normal.
  • White, green, gray, or dark fuzzy growth in the core: discard the apple.
  • Musty or fermented odor: discard.
  • Wet or decomposed flesh around the core: discard.

A clean-looking peel cannot rule out a problem that began in the center. Once you find true mold in the apple's core, throwing away the whole fruit is the simplest safe decision.

faq.question: Why can an apple be moldy inside but look fine outside?
faq.answer: Some fungi colonize the seed cavity first, so visible symptoms may remain hidden until the apple is cut.

faq.question: Can I cut out a moldy apple core and eat the rest?
faq.answer: It is safer to discard the whole apple because visible internal mold does not show how far fungal growth or tissue damage has extended.

faq.question: Do black apple seeds mean the core is moldy?
faq.answer: No. Mature seeds can be naturally dark; mold appears as fuzzy, cottony, or powdery growth in the cavity.
